items.title: Jim Cullum interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007
items.q: everybody is fascinated by Charlie Parker, myself included.

ctx.x: Okay, part two. Did anybody say anything this morning or could you add anything about making traditional jazz more a part of the jazz education scene?

Well that’s what we’re interested in seeing happen and it’s one of the reasons that I’m here at IAJE. We would love to see, as time goes by, traditional jazz or earlier forms of jazz sort of like Wycliffe Gordon was alluding to some of these things today, the full spectrum of jazz, from its origins to the most avante garde modern day manifestations of the music, be on display and be present in jazz education. And for most, in the vast majority of cases with jazz education, the attitude has been we start with…

new idea. And the fact that we now have that idea on the table changes the game a little bit. And now everybody’s going to say, “Hmm, maybe we better look at this thing again and look at it a little differently.” And as far as I’m concerned I’d say it’s about time that everybody takes a good hard look at jazz. Where did it come from? How did this thing happen anyway? And let’s look at the whole picture of the whole history of it. Because, hey, Charlie Parker is now sixty years old. That music is getting to be,…
